title: White Sox to sign Dustin May to 3-year-deal, boosting their rotation: Sources
author: Andrew Baggarly
content:
A pitching-starved Chicago White Sox team that exceeded expectations in 2026 has made the first leap into the rotation free-agent market by agreeing Tuesday to a long-term contract with veteran right-hander Dustin May.

May will sign a three-year, $52.5 million deal, according to league sources who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the deal was not official. FanSided first reported news of the agreement.

The 29-year-old will slot into the middle of Chicago’s rotation. May became a free agent when he turned down his end of a $20 million mutual option with the Milwaukee Brewers. It wasn’t much of a gamble, though.

There were plenty of reasons for May to feel confident betting on himself. He throws a six-pitch mix, and his fastball ranked in the 85th percentile in MLB with an average velocity of 96.8 mph, making him an intriguing ingredient for any franchise that has confidence in its ability to polish up a pitcher with plus raw stuff.

May’s contract establishes the bar for a mid-rotation starter, and it’s a deal that should encourage those pitchers. Free-agent starters might have one of the deeper pools of available targets this offseason. Clay Holmes, Michael Soroka, Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, Tyler Mahle, Nick Martinez and Foster Griffin can all make cases as mid-rotation stabilizers like May. Many of them could argue they’re worth more than him.

The White Sox could still pursue more rotation fortifications, but May — whose $52.5 million guarantee is the largest sum the White Sox have given a free-agent starting pitcher since Dallas Keuchel’s $55.5 million in December 2019 — upgrades their group. They have holdovers Sean Burke, Davis Martin and Anthony Kay — the three pitchers who led them in innings a season ago. They intend to make Grant Taylor a starter in 2027. Luis Castillo, a trade acquisition last summer who flopped, is under contract for another season.

Chicago made the postseason despite a rotation with a 4.60 ERA that ranked 26th in MLB. The White Sox used 18 starting pitchers, often deploying an opener to cover two rotation spots. Their lack of pitching depth was particularly felt in the postseason when their best arms hit a wall after frequent usage.

May, whom the Brewers acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals at last season’s trade deadline, showcased his abilities on June 15, when he tossed a one-hit shutout against the San Diego Padres at Busch Stadium. The nine-strikeout gem was the only complete game by a Cardinals pitcher all season.

Although nothing about May’s recent statistics jumps off the page — he had a 4.70 ERA in 31 starts last season — there’s never been any question about his ceiling when he stays healthy. That’s what he did in 2026, throwing a career-high 145 2/3 innings with the Cardinals and Brewers, then contributing on the mound in each of the Brewers’ three postseason series on the way to the club’s first World Series title.

The key has been staying on the mound. May wasn’t able to do that in six years with the Los Angeles Dodgers after making a ballyhooed debut as a 21-year-old prospect in 2019. He underwent Tommy John surgery in 2021, then had a second elbow ligament reconstruction along with a flexor tendon repair in 2023. While in the final stages of rehab from those surgeries in 2024, he suffered an even scarier injury: a ruptured esophagus when a piece of lettuce got caught in his throat, which required emergency surgery.
